note: Sample data only. Shown when no YT_KEY is set. Titles, channels and thumbnails are invented.

items.title: Newton's laws, drawn on a free-body diagram
items.description: Why the second law is a statement about acceleration rather than force, worked through four free-body diagrams: a block on a ramp, a hanging mass, a pulley, and a car turning a corner.

items.title: Electrostatics: field lines without the hand-waving
items.description: Where the field line picture comes from, what it can and cannot tell you, and three configurations drawn slowly enough to follow.

items.title: Ray optics: one lens, four cases
items.description: The thin lens equation derived once, then applied to the four positions of an object relative to the focal point.

items.title: SN1 versus SN2: the two substitution pathways side by side
items.description: Rate laws, stereochemistry and solvent effects, compared on the same substrate so the difference is visible rather than memorised.

items.title: Carbonyl chemistry: nucleophilic addition and its reversals
items.description: One mechanism, many named reactions. Why almost everything a carbonyl does is the same addition followed by a different collapse.

items.title: Aromaticity and Hückel's rule, without the hand-waving
items.description: Where the 4n+2 rule comes from, what counts as a ring current, and four molecules that look aromatic but are not.

items.title: Chemical kinetics: order, rate constants and half-life
items.description: Zero, first and second order integrated rate laws derived, then read off three real concentration-time plots.

items.title: Equilibrium: what a large K actually tells you
items.description: Le Chatelier as a consequence of the equilibrium constant rather than a separate rule, with the pressure and temperature cases separated.

items.title: Electrochemistry: cells, potentials and the Nernst equation
items.description: Standard potentials, how they combine, and why a cell voltage changes as it discharges. Worked with a Daniell cell first.

items.title: Periodic trends: why the table is shaped the way it is
items.description: Effective nuclear charge, shielding and radius, then the three trends that follow from them and the exceptions worth knowing.

items.title: Coordination compounds: naming, geometry and isomerism
items.description: A naming system built from the inside out, then the geometries that actually occur and the isomerism each one allows.

items.title: The p-block, group by group
items.description: Anomalies first, then the trends that explain them: inert pair effect, catenation, and the diagonal relationship.

items.title: Human physiology: one breath, step by step
items.description: From the diaphragm to the alveolus and back, with the pressure changes that drive each stage.

items.title: Animal kingdom: the body plans that separate the phyla
items.description: Symmetry, segmentation and coelom, used as three questions that place almost any animal in the right group.

items.title: Genetics: from a cross to a ratio
items.description: Mendel's crosses worked with a Punnett square, then the deviations: linkage, incomplete dominance, and lethal alleles.

items.title: Photosynthesis: the light reactions, step by step
items.description: Photosystems, the electron transport chain and the proton gradient, drawn once and then labelled.

items.title: Plant morphology: reading a flower
items.description: A flower dissected in order, with the terms for each whorl and the family differences they reveal.

items.title: Plant physiology: how water reaches the top of a tree
items.description: Root pressure, cohesion-tension and transpiration, with the numbers that make the second one the only workable answer.
